variants.title: Give each part its job
variants.context: LMSYS Arena evaluation is a human-evaluation method in which a person sees two anonymous model responses to the same prompt and chooses A, B, a tie, or neither. Many pairwise votes are aggregated into estimates of which models people prefer.
variants.prompt: From the lesson section “What does an arena result measure?”: match each part to its responsibility.

pairs.label: Relative
pairs.detail: A score changes when the opponent pool changes.
pairs.explanation: A score changes when the opponent pool changes. Beating weak opponents is not the same evidence as beating strong ones.

pairs.label: Conditional
pairs.detail: The prompt languages, domains, difficulty, voter population, and interface define the population to which the result applies.
pairs.explanation: The prompt languages, domains, difficulty, voter population, and interface define the population to which the result applies.

pairs.label: Probabilistic
pairs.detail: A rating is an estimate with sampling uncertainty.
pairs.explanation: A rating is an estimate with sampling uncertainty. Nearby ranks may be statistically indistinguishable.

variants.hint: Give each part the one job only it can do, then rule out the rest. An arena result is relative and conditional.
variants.explanation: Each part has a distinct responsibility. Relative: A score changes when the opponent pool changes. Conditional: The prompt languages, domains, difficulty, voter population, and interface define the population to which the result applies. Probabilistic: A rating is an estimate with sampling uncertainty.

pairs.label: Sample a prompt and pair

pairs.label: Generate comparably
pairs.detail: Use the same prompt and disclose material differences in system instructions, tools, temperature, token limits, and latency policy.

pairs.detail: Hide identity, swap left and right placement, permit ties or both-bad outcomes, and retain the assignment metadata.
pairs.explanation: Hide identity, swap left and right placement, permit ties or both-bad outcomes, and retain the assignment metadata.

pairs.label: Filter and estimate
pairs.detail: Remove invalid events with auditable rules, aggregate pairwise outcomes, bootstrap or model uncertainty, and publish slice-level diagnostics.

variants.title: Make the decision
variants.context: LMSYS Arena evaluation is a human-evaluation method in which a person sees two anonymous model responses to the same prompt and chooses A, B, a tie, or neither. Many pairwise votes are aggregated into estimates of which models people prefer.
variants.prompt: What does an arena preference score establish most directly?
options: How often sampled voters preferred one model over its opponents under the evaluated conditions
That the highest-rated model is factually correct on every prompt
That the leading model satisfies every product safety policy
The absolute quality of a model independently of its opponents
variants.explanation: Arena evidence is relative and conditional on the opponents, prompts, voters, interface, and time window. It does not establish absolute correctness or safety.

variants.hint: Think about the key idea first: In plain language: an arena asks, "Which response would this voter rather receive for this prompt?" It does not ask whether a model is universally correct, safe, fast, or suitable for your product.

variants.title: Make the decision
variants.context: LMSYS Arena evaluation is a human-evaluation method in which a person sees two anonymous model responses to the same prompt and chooses A, B, a tie, or neither. Many pairwise votes are aggregated into estimates of which models people prefer.
variants.prompt: Candidate A is always shown on the left, and voters have a stable left-side preference. What happens as the arena collects many more votes without changing placement?
options: The interval narrows around a systematically shifted estimate
The true preference automatically converges to exactly 50%
The opponent pool no longer affects the rating
variants.explanation: More votes reduce sampling uncertainty, but they do not repair systematic assignment bias. The arena can become more confident about the wrong value.

variants.title: Make the decision
variants.context: LMSYS Arena evaluation is a human-evaluation method in which a person sees two anonymous model responses to the same prompt and chooses A, B, a tie, or neither. Many pairwise votes are aggregated into estimates of which models people prefer.
variants.prompt: Candidate A has 190 wins, Candidate B has 150 wins, and there are 60 ties. If ties are split evenly, what is A's preference score?
variants.explanation: A earns 190 + 0.5 x 60 = 220 points from 400 votes, so its split-tie score is 220 / 400 = 55%.

variants.context: LMSYS Arena evaluation is a human-evaluation method in which a person sees two anonymous model responses to the same prompt and chooses A, B, a tie, or neither. Many pairwise votes are aggregated into estimates of which models people prefer.
variants.prompt: A pairwise estimate is 54%, but its 95% interval runs from 49% to 59%. What is the defensible interpretation?
options: The matchup is unresolved because the interval includes an even 50% result
Candidate A is definitively better because 54% exceeds 50%
Candidate B is definitively better because the lower bound is below 50%
The confidence interval proves that the prompt sample is representative
variants.explanation: The interval includes 50%, so sampling uncertainty is large enough that a strict winner is not supported. Representativeness is a separate design question.

variants.prompt: A candidate has a statistically supported arena lead. Which additional evidence is required before a production release?
options: Product-representative correctness, safety, latency, cost, and policy gates followed by a bounded canary
No additional evidence because preference subsumes every product requirement
A public rank without model-version or data-window metadata
variants.explanation: Preference is one evaluation channel. Release decisions also need product-specific hard gates and a controlled rollout with rollback thresholds.
